title: Jaundice: interpretation of liver blood tests

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee in the surgical assessment unit. A 67-year-old patient has yellow eyes and dark urine for 10 days, pale stools, generalised itch and 4 kg unintentional weight loss. Observations: 36.8°C, HR 84, BP 132/76 mmHg. They are alert, without abdominal tenderness. Provided data: Bilirubin 116 µmol/L (3–20); ALP 612 U/L (30–130); GGT 480 U/L (10–60); ALT 92 U/L (0–45); AST 74 U/L (0–40); albumin 38 g/L (35–50); INR 1.0 (0.9–1.2); haemoglobin 129 g/L; WCC 7.6 × 10⁹/L. Local laboratory ranges are shown. Ultrasound is not yet performed.
brief.task: Interpret the provided liver blood results; explain your differential, immediate investigations and safe referral pathway. Respond to additional results supplied by the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Cholestatic jaundice with red flags for malignant obstruction; distinguish pattern, synthetic function, urgency and next investigation.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Equating ALP with cancer, or ordering ERCP before establishing the cause in a well patient with suspicious obstruction.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: “This is a predominantly cholestatic pattern: bilirubin, ALP and GGT are raised out of proportion to aminotransferases. I would first assess for cholangitis or liver failure.”

flow: Identify cholestatic pattern and synthetic function
Assess danger signs and relevant history
Request ultrasound and appropriate further imaging/referral
Respond to deterioration and close with a clear handover

grid.label: Pattern
grid.fail: Mislabels as hepatitic despite marked ALP/GGT
grid.borderline: Calls jaundice but gives no pattern
grid.pass: Identifies predominantly cholestatic profile and uses the printed ranges
grid.high: States mixed elevation possible and distinguishes pattern from diagnosis

grid.label: Severity
grid.fail: Ignores haemodynamic or mental-state red flags
grid.pass: Checks for fever, pain, confusion, shock and bleeding
grid.high: Articulates cholangitis/sepsis and synthetic-failure escalation triggers

grid.label: Function
grid.fail: Calls normal INR/albumin proof of a healthy liver
grid.pass: Distinguishes synthetic function (INR/albumin) from injury/cholestasis tests
grid.high: Notes albumin changes slowly and normal results do not exclude serious disease

grid.label: Differential
grid.pass: Considers choledocholithiasis, biliary stricture, pancreatic/biliary malignancy and intrahepatic cholestasis
grid.high: Connects painless weight loss/pruritus to malignancy without prematurely diagnosing it

grid.label: History
grid.pass: Asks fever, pain, stool/urine colour, weight change, drug history and prior biliary disease
grid.high: Adds autoimmune risk, alcohol, surgery, hepatitis history and trend of prior tests

grid.label: Imaging
grid.fail: Orders ERCP as universal first test
grid.borderline: Suggests an ultrasound without explaining next step
grid.pass: Requests urgent ultrasound; then targeted cross-sectional imaging according to findings
grid.high: Explains why suspicious pancreatic obstruction needs pancreas-protocol CT before biliary drainage when stable

grid.label: Referral
grid.fail: Reassures despite jaundice and weight loss
grid.pass: Identifies suspected-cancer pathway for patient aged ≥40 with jaundice, and communicates to senior team
grid.high: Coordinates hepatobiliary/upper GI MDT and investigations without causing avoidable delays

grid.label: Deterioration
grid.fail: Defers care when sepsis cue develops
grid.pass: Recognises new fever, rigors and hypotension as possible cholangitis; activates sepsis assessment and urgent biliary discussion
grid.high: Orders cultures before antibiotics if no treatment delay, IV treatment per local policy and urgent source control with senior support

grid.label: Closure
grid.pass: Summarises pattern, investigation, escalation and safety-netting
grid.high: Provides structured referral including observations, results and change in condition

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What pattern do you see?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: ALT is elevated so it must be hepatitis. I would repeat the panel next month.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The bilirubin and ALP are markedly high; does that alter your view?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Not really. The ALT is the main issue.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The INR and albumin are normal. What does that tell you?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That proves the liver is healthy, so this cannot be serious.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you like to know anything else about how the patient is?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, the blood results are all I need; I will not check for fever, confusion or bleeding.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What history is important?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Has the patient had alcohol?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: No significant alcohol intake. What will you do next?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would book an ERCP as the first test; there is no need for an ultrasound.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Ultrasound shows dilated ducts and an indistinct pancreatic head.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That is probably gallstones. We can wait until an ERCP appointment becomes available.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: They develop rigors, temperature 38.7°C, HR 116 and BP 88/54. What now?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The bloods are already abnormal, so I would monitor and wait for a scan tomorrow.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Do you wish to escalate?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Not yet, I do not think it is urgent.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please summarise and hand over.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: There is nothing to hand over; the day team can sort it out tomorrow.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Interpret these liver blood tests.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Bilirubin 116, ALP 612 and GGT 480 with a smaller ALT rise to 92 indicate predominantly cholestatic jaundice, not an isolated hepatocellular pattern.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What about albumin 38 and INR 1.0?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: These do not show impaired synthesis at present, but they do not exclude serious obstruction or cancer.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What would you ask?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would ask about pain, fever and rigors; dark urine, pale stools, itch, weight loss, appetite, drugs, alcohol, previous gallstones and biliary procedures.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No pain or fever so far; there is weight loss, pale stools and itch.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: They are stable at present. I would document observations and check for new fever, hypotension, confusion or abdominal pain, which would require urgent escalation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Give your differential.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Extrahepatic obstruction from stones, benign stricture or pancreatic/biliary malignancy is important. Intrahepatic drug-related or autoimmune cholestasis is possible.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What imaging would you request?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urgent abdominal ultrasound for duct dilatation and biliary pathology, alongside senior discussion and review of prior tests and medicines.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ultrasound shows dilated ducts, CBD 13 mm and indistinct pancreatic head.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is suspicious for distal biliary obstruction. If pancreatic cancer is suspected, I would arrange pancreatic-protocol CT before biliary drainage while the patient is stable, with hepatobiliary input.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What referral?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: They are 67 with jaundice, so meet the NICE NG12 suspected pancreatic cancer referral criterion. I would inform my registrar and coordinate the urgent pathway.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Now the nurse reports fever 38.7°C, HR 116 and BP 88/54 with rigors.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is a new emergency: possible ascending cholangitis and sepsis. I would call for urgent senior help, begin ABCDE, IV access, bloods including lactate and cultures if timely, IV antibiotics per local guideline and monitored resuscitation, and urgently discuss biliary drainage.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please finish.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will hand over the obstructive jaundice, ultrasound findings, suspected cause and new shock physiology, requesting immediate review and source-control planning.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: You are given this report. Where do you start?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: First I check whether the patient is unwell now: vitals, fever or rigors, RUQ pain, mental state, haemodynamic instability and evidence of bleeding or encephalopathy.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: They are afebrile, haemodynamically stable and alert.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The dominant abnormality is cholestasis: ALP 612 and GGT 480, bilirubin 116, with less prominent ALT 92 and AST 74. I would not label the cause from enzyme magnitude alone.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Are their liver functions preserved?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Albumin 38 and INR 1.0 are currently reassuring regarding synthetic function, although albumin is slow-changing and neither normal result rules out malignancy or obstruction.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What targeted history matters?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would establish onset and progression, biliary pain, fever, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, weight loss, appetite, previous stones or ERCP, operations, drug/supplement exposure and earlier LFTs.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: They confirm ten days of jaundice, pale stools and 4 kg weight loss, without pain.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Painless cholestatic jaundice with weight loss raises distal malignant obstruction, including pancreatic head cancer, but I would retain common bile duct stone, cholangiocarcinoma, benign stricture and intrahepatic cholestasis.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Which investigation first?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Urgent ultrasound to establish whether ducts are dilated; I would also review prior LFTs, FBC, renal function and the clinical aetiology screen where appropriate rather than reflexively repeating an isolated panel.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Ultrasound: CBD 13 mm, intra- and extrahepatic dilatation, indistinct pancreatic head.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That supports extrahepatic obstruction. I would promptly discuss a pancreatic-protocol CT before drainage in the stable patient, with specialist MDT input; ERCP is not a diagnostic reflex before CT.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How urgent is referral?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: NICE NG12 recommends the suspected-cancer pathway for a person aged 40 or over with jaundice. I would contact the senior surgical/hepatobiliary team today, ensure the pathway is activated, and avoid telling the patient this proves cancer.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The nurse now reports 38.7°C, rigors, HR 116 and BP 88/54.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The priority changes immediately. I would initiate ABCDE and a sepsis response, seek consultant/critical-care support, obtain blood cultures if this does not delay antimicrobials, give IV antibiotics and carefully titrated fluids with reassessment, and arrange urgent biliary decompression with the responsible team.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What would you tell the next clinician?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: “A 67-year-old with obstructive cholestatic jaundice, duct dilatation and possible pancreatic head lesion has now developed probable cholangitis with shock. Please review immediately for resuscitation and urgent biliary source control; we have started the sepsis bundle and are monitoring response.”

failures.move: Failing to recognise the late shock/rigors cue and delaying urgent escalation.
failures.consequence: Potential delay of treatment for biliary sepsis and source control.

failures.move: Ordering immediate invasive drainage without appropriate prior imaging in a stable suspected pancreatic malignancy.
failures.consequence: May compromise staging or create avoidable procedure risk.

failures.move: Reassuring the jaundiced, weight-losing patient without timely senior/specialist referral.

recovery.line: I concentrated on ALT and missed that ALP, GGT and bilirubin dominate. This is cholestatic; I will reassess obstruction and urgency.
The new fever and hypotension change the station: I am stopping the elective plan and initiating urgent sepsis care and biliary escalation.

knowledge.fact: Bilirubin, ALP, GGT and ALT are interpreted together; clinical history and trends matter.
ALP with raised GGT supports a hepatobiliary source rather than isolated bone ALP.
Abnormal tests can be significant even if the magnitude is modest; synthetic markers are a separate question.
Abdominal ultrasound forms part of the standard adult abnormal-liver-test aetiology assessment.
At age 40 or above with jaundice, use a suspected-cancer referral pathway for pancreatic cancer.
In suspected pancreatic cancer with obstructive jaundice, obtain pancreas-protocol CT before biliary drainage when clinically appropriate.

recall.think: Is this obstructive cholestasis, and is the patient septic now?
recall.say: “The pattern is cholestatic; the cause remains to be established.”
do: Check stability, obtain ultrasound, coordinate appropriate cross-sectional imaging and referral.

numbers.meaning: Age with jaundice: NG12 suspected-cancer referral
case CBD is dilated, interpreted clinically

recall.trap: Painless jaundice is not harmless; ERCP is not the default first diagnostic test.
recall.finish: Handover the changed physiology and explicit source-control plan.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Explains why suspicious pancreatic obstruction needs pancreas-protocol CT before biliary drainage when stable
